newsitem.title: UK: Italian lira extends slump after tough EMU comments.
newsitem.headline: Italian lira extends slump after tough EMU comments.

text.p: The lira sagged further on Wednesday and stood some 13 lire down against the mark on the week after tough EMU comments out of Germany sparked a run on the currency, analysts said.

The Italian currency fell nearly nine lire on Tuesday after a German government official said some EMU aspirants would be well advised to delay entry into the single currency and was declining again on Wednesday.
"The speculators are getting out of lira," said a trader at a UK bank.
At 1247 GMT the lira stood at 986.10 against 980.50 in late Europe on Tuesday and down over 13 lire from Monday's close at 972.58 lire.
Analysts and traders said comments on Tuesday by State secretary to the German Finance Ministry Juergen Stark helped to ignite a lira sell-off from speculators who were already long of the currency.
"The weight of positions certainly favours liquidation of lira positions," said Nick Parsons, forex strategist at Banque Paribas.

Stark said some qualifiers should forsake the political prestige of joining economic and monetary union (EMU) at the outset. "There are some members whose economic structures are not yet well enough prepared to take part," he said.
While Stark did not name names, his comments appeared directed at countries like Italy or Spain.
"He (Stark) was suggesting that the Germans do not really want to have Italy or Spain in monetary union," said Ernesto Ramirez, analyst at Bankers Trust.
"The price to be paid for a single currency will be the exclusion of the lira - temporarily - for 12 months," said Paribas' Parsons.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, while acknowledging the depth of German public disquiet on at the prospect of Italian membership of Europe's single currency, said he would take every step to dispel the doubts.

Reaffirming Italy's intention to be among founder members of the new euro from 1999, Prodi on Tuesday proposed moving the deadline for parliamentary passage of the country's 1998 budget forward by four months to mid-August to boost confidence.

He said the move not only would reassure financial markets that Italy was serious about putting its finances in order but would also give "German voters and the German political world a pretty long time" to consider the country's merits.
But analysts say it is unlikely that Germany will accept Italy in EMU at the incept.
"There is fear within the electorate (German) that Italy is not a stable country in terms of politics and fiscal policy," said Ramirez.
"That they (Germans) have to give up the D-mark for a more inflation-prone currency would definitely not be a palatable choice for them," he added.

And while analysts said Stark's comment could also be seen to affect Spain, the Spanish peseta - down two pesetas at 84.64 on Wednesday - was not as badly hit as the lira, partly, because it is not as liquid.
And, say analysts, the fact that the Spanish budget deficit and inflation targets are much closer than those required by Maastricht.
"Spain is one of the best bets among the outsiders. We don't think it will join on day one but has a better economic case for membership than Italy does," said Parsons.

With the focus on the lira, traders are now looking at where the fall will be couched. Traders said 990 - the mark/lira's central parity rate in the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) - would be good support.
"I think the mark will get offered by the bank of Italy at 985 lire, that would be a level were they would start coming in," said one currency analyst.
Parsons said from a technical perspective, there is some resistance at 985 and 987 lire.
"But we think it will settle above its central (ERM) rate...We don't see the lira being able to sustain a position stronger than its central rate," he added.
